passage:
In the courtyard behind her mother's tailoring shop, Vandana held her phone at arm's length and frowned. The filter smoothed her cheeks and widened her eyes. Without it, the camera showed a pimple and a crooked smile, and she thought, that can't be me.
"Leave that thing, race me to the mango tree," said Madhuri, dragging her off the step. They ran until Vandana was breathless and laughing, and she noticed how far her legs had carried her.
That evening she unfollowed two accounts full of edited faces and followed a girl who posts kabaddi videos. She still looked in the mirror for a long time, but the crooked smile was at least her own.

qa.q: Whom did Vandana follow after unfollowing the two accounts of edited faces?
qa.a: She followed a girl who posts kabaddi videos.

qa.q: What did Vandana think when the camera showed her without the filter?
qa.a: She thought "that can't be me", which shows the edited image had made her real face feel wrong.

qa.q: How did racing to the mango tree help Vandana?
qa.a: It moved her attention to what her body can do, not only how it looks, and she ended up breathless and laughing.

qa.q: How might Madhuri have seen Vandana's frown at the phone?
qa.a: Madhuri may have noticed a friend being unkind to herself and chose a simple way to pull her out of it without a speech.

grounding: Shows a teen whose filtered images make her real face feel wrong, turning to real people and what her body can do.

passage:
School counsellor's note, Class 10, Friday

Aditi came in after her class teacher noticed she had stopped taking part in the class photo. She showed me her phone. Every picture of herself used a beauty filter: smoother skin, a thinner nose, bigger eyes. "Without it, my face looks wrong," she said. "Like it's broken." She would not look up.

I did not argue with her feelings. I showed her a short video about how magazine and influencer photos are edited, layer by layer. She watched with her mouth open. "That's not even the same person."

I asked what she enjoys doing, rather than how she looks. She said she used to love dancing before she got self-conscious. I suggested the school's folk dance group, where her classmate Manjula practises every Wednesday.

I also asked her to try a week of following people who post unfiltered photos, and to tell me how it felt.

She came back on Friday. She had joined the dance group. "My feet hurt," she said, and smiled.

qa.q: What did Aditi's filter change in her pictures?
qa.a: It gave her smoother skin, a thinner nose and bigger eyes.

qa.q: What was Aditi feeling when she said her face looked broken?
qa.a: Aditi felt deeply insecure and ashamed of her real face, unable to look up.

qa.q: How did the counsellor help Aditi shift her focus?
qa.a: The counsellor showed how images are edited, suggested following people who post unfiltered photos, and pointed her to the dance group so she could enjoy what her body can do.

qa.q: How might Manjula feel when Aditi joins the dance group?
qa.a: Manjula would probably feel glad to have a classmate practising with her on Wednesdays.

grounding: It shows a teen for whom filters make her real face look wrong, learning that images are engineered, following real people and spending time on what her body can do.

passage:
Saturday

I did an experiment today. I took one selfie without the filter and one with it. With the filter, I look like a doll. Without it, I look like me, and for a whole year I'd decided "me" was ugly.

I scrolled through the girls I follow. Every face perfect. Then I found a tiny "edited" note on one of them, and another had posted a "before" photo by mistake. Pores. Dark circles. A real person.

So I unfollowed eleven accounts and followed a swimmer, a woman who makes pottery, and a travel account that never uses filters.

Then Alka called and asked if I wanted to go swimming. I nearly said no because of the costume. I went anyway.

We raced four lengths. I lost, but I laughed so hard I swallowed water. Walking home, my arms were aching and I didn't think about my face once.

My body swam four lengths today. That's what I want to remember.

Ishita

qa.q: How many accounts did Ishita unfollow?
What was Ishita feeling about the unfiltered selfie before the experiment?
qa.a: Ishita felt insecure and ashamed, having decided for a whole year that the real face in the mirror was ugly.

qa.q: What did Ishita do that helped, and why?
qa.a: Ishita unfollowed edited accounts, followed real people and went swimming with Alka, which shifted the focus to what Ishita's body can do.

qa.q: How might Alka feel about Ishita coming swimming?
qa.a: Alka probably felt happy and had fun, since they raced and laughed together.

grounding: It shows a teen who feels filters make their real face look wrong, learning that images are engineered, following real people and enjoying what their body can do.
